decision.location: Materials and Methods, page 9, lines 503-516 (and Discussion, page 14, lines 782-794)
decision.quote:
Noise-Vocoded Lexically Controlled Words and Sentences—The stimulus lists of
lexically controlled words and sentences originally developed by Eisenberg et al. (2002)
were used to investigate the effects of word frequency and neighborhood density on word
recognition in isolation and in sentences. Eisenberg et al. (2002) created two lists of words
based on lexical competition: one lexically “easy” list and one lexically “hard” list. Each list
consisted of 15 practice words followed by 60 test words produced by one female speaker.
The easy and hard word lists were then combined to create one set of 30 practice words and
120 test words that were noise-vocoded and presented in a randomized order. Practice trials
always preceded test trials (see PDF, Supplemental Digital Content 1). For the word
recognition task, children were instructed to repeat what they heard out loud to the
experimenter. No feedback was provided regarding response accuracy.
Eisenberg et al. (2002) also created two lists of 25 low-predictability sentences (5 practice
and 20 test sentences) using the same easy and hard words that were produced by one
female speaker and previously presented in isolation (see Bell & Wilson, 2001).
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. In Part I ('Part I: Replication of Eisenberg et al. (2002)'), Roman et al. (2017) directly replicate Experiment 2 of Eisenberg et al. (2002) (retained shipped input_row_index '622', DOI 10.1097/00003446-200210000-00007) using the pediatric word and sentence lists created by Eisenberg et al. (2002). Bell and Wilson (2001) is cited in Methods as the adult sentence-materials precursor that Eisenberg et al. (2002) adapted and in a single Discussion sentence noting that the Eisenberg et al. (2002) replication results also parallel Bell and Wilson (2001) with adults, without any separate empirical test in Results. Per the codebook replication-chain and materials-source rules, Part I's retested target is already represented by shipped row '622' (Eisenberg et al., 2002).

corrected_value.title: Talker discrimination by prelingually deaf children with cochlear implants: Preliminary results

decision.location: Discussion, page 16, lines 894-900 (with task design in Methods, pages 10-11, lines 563-603; empirical tests in Results, pages 13-14, lines 741-765; and full citation in References, page 19, lines 1081-1082)
decision.quote:
Results from the TD task also replicated findings from the earlier study of deaf children with
CIs carried out by Cleary and Pisoni (2002). They found much better performance on the
fixed-sentence condition than the varied-sentence condition and stronger correlations
between performance on the fixed-sentence condition and several conventional speech
recognition measures. A similar pattern was also found in the error rates for each condition
in the present study with a much stronger response bias for committing false alarms
observed during the more difficult varied-sentence condition.
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. In Part II of the study, Roman et al. (2017) administer a 4-channel noise-vocoded adaptation of the Talker Discrimination (TD) task modeled after Cleary and Pisoni (2002) (Annals of Otology, Rhinology, & Laryngology 2002; 111(5 Part 2):113-118) using sentence pairs from the Indiana Multi-Talker Sentence Database. In Results (lines 741-765, Table 3) and Discussion (lines 894-900), they empirically test and directly compare three specific findings from Cleary and Pisoni (2002): (1) significantly higher talker-discrimination accuracy in the fixed-sentence condition than in the varied-sentence condition (t(31)=4.76, p<.001), (2) stronger correlations between the fixed-sentence condition and spoken word recognition measures (rs=.49 and .51, p<.01) than for the varied-sentence condition (rs=.39 and .40, p<.05), and (3) a doubled false-alarm rate in the varied-sentence condition relative to the fixed-sentence condition (23.11% vs. 11.54%, t(30)=-.464, p<.001). The sole shipped row (input_row_index '622', Eisenberg et al., 2002, Ear and Hearing, DOI 10.1097/00003446-200210000-00007) investigated lexically controlled word and sentence recognition and did not include talker discrimination, so report equivalence does not apply and Cleary and Pisoni (2002) is a genuinely absent replication target.

corrected_value.title: Does time of day affect variety-seeking?

decision.location: Abstract, line 37 (and Background, lines 72-87; Method and Results, lines 96-185; Discussion, lines 188-198; References, lines 205-209)
decision.quote: To shed light on the different findings, we carry out a replication using a unique dataset from the UK, which tracks individual purchases of food and drinks for out of home consumption over a period of three years. Similar to Gullo et al. (2019), we found variety-seeking increases from the morning to the afternoon. Additionally, we found a post-lunch dip. Our results as such lend further support to the matching mechanism between variety-seeking and diurnal level proposed by Gullo et al. (2019) rather than the compensating mechanism suggested by Roehm and Roehm (2004).
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. Luna triage mistakenly conflated target_index 1 (Gullo et al., 2019) with the sibling target Roehm and Roehm (2004) (shipped row '1493'). In fact, Trinh (2025) explicitly frames and conducts the study as an empirical replication designed to adjudicate the conflicting time-of-day variety-seeking findings of both Roehm and Roehm (2004) and Gullo, Berger, Etkin, and Bollinger (2019, Journal of Consumer Research 46(1):20-35, DOI 10.1093/jcr/ucy061). Specifically, Trinh (2025) retests Gullo et al.'s (2019) full-day (6 am to 11 pm) continuous non-linear diurnal pattern using polynomial regressions across three variety-seeking measures (brand count, Entropy, and reversed HHI; Figs. 1-3, Table 1), confirming Gullo et al.'s finding that variety-seeking increases from morning to early afternoon (6 am to 1 pm) and supporting Gullo et al.'s diurnal matching mechanism. The sole shipped row (input_row_index '1493', Roehm & Roehm, 2004, Marketing Letters 15:213-221, DOI 10.1007/s11002-005-0457-y) is a separate 2004 paper by different authors in a different journal reporting the opposite effect, so report equivalence does not apply and Gullo et al. (2019) is a genuinely absent replication target.
